subproblems.title: C¹ cover of a countably n-rectifiable set by bi-Lipschitz ball pieces (Simon Ch. 3, Lemma 1.2 'only if'; reused accepted declaration)
subproblems.statement: Let P, n ∈ ℕ and let M ⊆ ℝ^P be countably n-rectifiable (SimonGMT CountablyRectifiable n M). Then there are C¹ maps g_k : ℝ^n → ℝ^P, points c_k ∈ ℝ^n, reals r_k and constants m_k > 0 (k ∈ ℕ) such that, with N_k := g_k(B_{r_k}(c_k)) (the image of the open ball, which is empty when r_k ≤ 0): (i) m_k|a − b| ≤ |g_k(a) − g_k(b)| for all a, b ∈ B_{r_k}(c_k); (ii) each N_k is Borel; (iii) H^n(N_k) < ∞; (iv) H^n(M ∖ ⋃_k N_k) = 0. Here H^n = μHE[n].
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (P n : ℕ) (M : Set (Euclid P)), CountablyRectifiable n M → ∃ (g : ℕ → Euclid n → Euclid P) (c : ℕ → Euclid n) (r m : ℕ → ℝ), (∀ k, ContDiff ℝ 1 (g k)) ∧ (∀ k, 0 < m k) ∧ (∀ k, ∀ a ∈ ball (c k) (r k), ∀ b ∈ ball (c k) (r k), m k * ‖a - b‖ ≤ ‖g k a - g k b‖) ∧ (∀ k, MeasurableSet (g k '' ball (c k) (r k))) ∧ (∀ k, μHE[n] (g k '' ball (c k) (r k)) ≠ ∞) ∧ μHE[n] (M \ ⋃ k, g k '' ball (c k) (r k)) = 0

2. (The accepted argument.) It is Simon Ch. 3, Lemma 1.2 'only if', with the errata of the supplied proof: F_j(ℝⁿ) for 'graph F_j'; Lⁿ; Hⁿ(G({J = 0})) = 0; and submanifolds of ℝ^P. It runs as follows.
(a) By Definition 1.1, M ⊆ M₀ ∪ ⋃_j F_j(ℝⁿ) with Hⁿ(M₀) = 0 and each F_j Lipschitz.
(b) The C¹ Approximation Theorem (Ch. 2, 1.5), applied to the coordinates of F_j, gives C¹ maps G_{ij} with Lⁿ({F_j ≠ G_{ij}}) < 1/(i+1). So Z_j := ⋂_i {F_j ≠ G_{ij}} is Lⁿ-null and Hⁿ(F_j(Z_j)) = 0 (Lipschitz image). Hence F_j(ℝⁿ) ⊆ F_j(Z_j) ∪ ⋃_i G_{ij}(ℝⁿ).
(c) The critical image is null: Hⁿ(G_{ij}({DG_{ij} not injective})) = 0 by the area formula (SimonGMT area_image_criticalSet_eq_zero).
(d) Let x be a regular point, μ > 0 with |DG_{ij}(x)v| ≥ 2μ|v|, and δ_x > 0 with ‖DG_{ij}(y) − DG_{ij}(x)‖ ≤ μ on B_{δ_x}(x). The mean value inequality gives |G_{ij}(a) − G_{ij}(b)| ≥ μ|a − b| on B_{δ_x}(x). This is the bound (m_y/2)|a − b| of step 3 of the supplied proof.
(e) By Lindelöf, countably many balls cover the regular set: centres from a dense sequence, radii 1/(p+1), each ball inside some B_{δ_x}(x). Enumerating (j, i, ball) by k gives g_k, c_k, r_k, m_k, with r_k = 0 for unused indices.
(f) Properties (ii)–(iv):
- N_k is σ-compact, hence Borel.
- Hⁿ(N_k) < ∞, because g_k is Lipschitz on the closed ball.
- M ∖ ⋃_k N_k ⊆ M₀ ∪ ⋃_j F_j(Z_j) ∪ ⋃_{i,j} G_{ij}(critical set), which is Hⁿ-null.

3. (Role in this decomposition.) This child is steps 1–3 of the supplied proof of chart_pieces. The parent's charts (ψ_a, V_a) are (g_k, ball(c_k, r_k)). S_k := g_k(ball(c_k, r_k)) is Borel with finite H^{n+1}-measure, as chart_tangent requires. ∎

subproblems.title: C¹ Approximation Theorem for Lipschitz functions (Simon Ch. 2, Theorem 1.5; reused accepted declaration)
subproblems.statement: Let n ∈ ℕ, K ≥ 0 and let f : ℝ^n → ℝ be K-Lipschitz. Then for every ε ∈ (0, ∞] there is a C¹ function g : ℝ^n → ℝ with L^n({x : f(x) ≠ g(x)} ∪ {x : Df(x) ≠ Dg(x)}) < ε. Here ℝ^n = Euclid n, L^n is Lebesgue measure on it (volume), and Df(x) is the Fréchet derivative (Lean fderiv ℝ f x, which is 0 where f is not differentiable).

subproblems.statement: Let P, n ∈ ℕ, W ⊆ ℝ^P open, and A, B ⊆ ℝ^P Borel with Hⁿ(A ∩ K) < ∞ and Hⁿ(B ∩ K) < ∞ for every compact K ⊆ W (Hⁿ = μHE[n]). Then for Hⁿ-a.e. x ∈ ℝ^P: if x ∈ W, x ∈ A and x ∈ B, then for every linear subspace Q, HasApproximateTangentSpaceAt n A x Q ↔ HasApproximateTangentSpaceAt n B x Q.

2. (The accepted argument: Simon Ch. 3, Remark 1.5(2) and the proof of 1.6 '⇒', in symmetric form.)
(a) A ∖ B and B ∖ A are Borel and locally Hⁿ-finite in W. By the upper density theorem (Ch. 1, 3.6), ρ⁻ⁿHⁿ((A ∖ B) ∩ closedBall(x, ρ)) → 0 for Hⁿ-a.e. x ∈ W outside A ∖ B, and likewise for B ∖ A.
(b) Let x ∈ A ∩ B ∩ W be a point where both densities vanish, and choose r₀ > 0 with closedBall(x, r₀) ⊆ W.

subproblems.title: C¹ approximation of a Lipschitz function along one C¹ chart on compact Borel pieces (Simon Ch. 3, proof of 2.4; Ch. 2, Theorem 1.5)
subproblems.statement: Let P, N ∈ ℕ, let M ⊆ ℝ^P be Borel, f : ℝ^P → ℝ L-Lipschitz (L ≥ 0), ψ : ℝ^N → ℝ^P a C¹ map and V ⊆ ℝ^N open (ℝ^k = Euclid k). Then there are Borel sets Y_k ⊆ ℝ^N and C¹ functions F_k : ℝ^N → ℝ (k ∈ ℕ) such that for every k: closure(Y_k) is compact and contained in V, ψ(Y_k) ⊆ M, and f(ψ(y)) = F_k(y) for all y ∈ Y_k; moreover H^N((M ∩ ψ(V)) ∖ ⋃_k ψ(Y_k)) = 0, where H^N = μHE[N].
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (P N : ℕ) (M : Set (Euclid P)) (f : Euclid P → ℝ) (L : NNReal) (ψ : Euclid N → Euclid P) (V : Set (Euclid N)), MeasurableSet M → LipschitzWith L f → IsOpen V → ContDiff ℝ 1 ψ → ∃ (Y : ℕ → Set (Euclid N)) (F : ℕ → Euclid N → ℝ), (∀ k, ContDiff ℝ 1 (F k) ∧ MeasurableSet (Y k) ∧ IsCompact (closure (Y k)) ∧ closure (Y k) ⊆ V ∧ ψ '' Y k ⊆ M ∧ ∀ y ∈ Y k, f (ψ y) = F k y) ∧ μHE[N] ((M ∩ ψ '' V) \ ⋃ k, ψ '' Y k) = 0
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source. Steps 4–6 of the supplied proof of chart_pieces, for a single chart (ψ, V). That is the step of Simon's proof of Ch. 3, 2.4 (chapter-03.txt lines 375–378): 'decomposing Hⁿ-almost all M_j as a countable union if necessary and using the C¹ Approximation Theorem 1.5 of Ch. 2 … f|M_j = g_j|M_j, where g_j is C¹'.
- Sibling used: c1_approximation (Simon Ch. 2, Theorem 1.5; Lean codim1_rdo_c1_approximation).
- Change from the supplied step 4: it suffices that each compact piece lies in V, so the margin closedBall(q, 2ρ) ⊆ V_a is dropped. Tangent planes are handled on the whole chart ball by the sibling chart_tangent.

Facts used:
- H^N = μHE[N] equals Lebesgue measure L^N = volume on ℝ^N (Mathlib EuclideanSpace.euclideanHausdorffMeasure_eq_volume).
- If φ is C-Lipschitz on a set A, then H^N(φ(Z)) ≤ C^N·H^N(Z) for every Z ⊆ A (SimonGMT Chapter02.euclideanHausdorffMeasure_image_le_of_lipschitzOn).

1. (Compact pieces of V.) There are compact sets K_m ⊆ V (m ∈ ℕ), possibly empty, with ⋃_m K_m = V.
- For instance, take the closed balls closedBall(q, ρ) ⊆ V with q ∈ ℚ^N and rational ρ > 0. They cover V: given y ∈ V, choose ε > 0 with ball(y, ε) ⊆ V, a rational ρ ∈ (0, ε/2) and q ∈ ℚ^N with |q − y| < ρ. Then y ∈ closedBall(q, ρ) ⊆ ball(y, 2ρ) ⊆ V.
- Enumerate these countably many balls; if there are none (V = ∅), put K_m := ∅.
- In Lean: SigmaCompactSpace.exists_compact_covering on the subtype V, which is locally compact by IsOpen.locallyCompactSpace; K_m is the image of the m-th set under the inclusion.

2. (ψ is Lipschitz on K_m.) A C¹ map is locally Lipschitz, hence Lipschitz on each compact set (ContDiff.locallyLipschitz, LocallyLipschitzOn.exists_lipschitzOnWith_of_compact). So ψ is C_m-Lipschitz on K_m for some C_m ≥ 0, and u := f∘ψ is (L·C_m)-Lipschitz on K_m.

3. (McShane extension.) Let ū_m : ℝ^N → ℝ be (L·C_m)-Lipschitz with ū_m = f∘ψ on K_m (LipschitzOnWith.extend_real).

4. (C¹ approximation.) For k ∈ ℕ, apply c1_approximation to ū_m with ε := (k + 1)⁻¹ > 0. This gives a C¹ function g_{m,k} : ℝ^N → ℝ with
 L^N({ū_m ≠ g_{m,k}}) ≤ L^N({x : ū_m(x) ≠ g_{m,k}(x) or Dū_m(x) ≠ Dg_{m,k}(x)}) < (k + 1)⁻¹.
(The supplied proof uses ε = 2^{−k}; any positive sequence tending to 0 works.)

5. (Null sets.) Put Z_m := K_m ∩ ⋂_k {ū_m ≠ g_{m,k}}.
- For every k, Z_m ⊆ {ū_m ≠ g_{m,k}}, so L^N(Z_m) < (k + 1)⁻¹. Hence L^N(Z_m) = 0, and H^N(Z_m) = 0.
- Since Z_m ⊆ K_m and ψ is C_m-Lipschitz on K_m, H^N(ψ(Z_m)) ≤ C_m^N·H^N(Z_m) = 0.

6. (The pieces.) Enumerate ℕ × ℕ by b ∈ ℕ, writing (m, k) = Nat.unpair b. Put
 Y_b := K_m ∩ {y : ū_m(y) = g_{m,k}(y)} ∩ ψ⁻¹(M), F_b := g_{m,k}.
(a) F_b is C¹ (step 4).
(b) Y_b is Borel:
- K_m is compact, hence closed;
- {ū_m = g_{m,k}} is closed, since both functions are continuous;
- ψ⁻¹(M) is Borel, since ψ is continuous and M is Borel.
(c) Y_b ⊆ K_m and K_m is closed, so closure(Y_b) ⊆ K_m ⊆ V. Being a closed subset of the compact K_m, closure(Y_b) is compact.
(d) ψ(Y_b) ⊆ M, because Y_b ⊆ ψ⁻¹(M).
(e) Let y ∈ Y_b. Then y ∈ K_m, so f(ψ(y)) = ū_m(y) by step 3, and ū_m(y) = g_{m,k}(y) = F_b(y).

7. (Coverage.) Let x ∈ (M ∩ ψ(V)) ∖ ⋃_b ψ(Y_b). Write x = ψ(y) with y ∈ V, and choose m with y ∈ K_m (step 1).
- Suppose y ∉ Z_m. Then ū_m(y) = g_{m,k}(y) for some k. Since also ψ(y) = x ∈ M, y ∈ Y_b for b := Nat.pair m k. Then x ∈ ψ(Y_b), a contradiction.
- Hence y ∈ Z_m and x ∈ ψ(Z_m).
So (M ∩ ψ(V)) ∖ ⋃_b ψ(Y_b) ⊆ ⋃_m ψ(Z_m). By step 5 and countable subadditivity, its H^N-measure is 0. ∎
proof_key_steps: Cover the open V by countably many compact sets K_m ⊆ V.
ψ is Lipschitz on each K_m; extend f∘ψ restricted to K_m to a Lipschitz ū_m on ℝ^N (McShane).
c1_approximation gives C¹ g_{m,k} with L^N({ū_m ≠ g_{m,k}}) < 1/(k+1); Z_m := K_m ∩ ⋂_k{ū_m ≠ g_{m,k}} is null, and so is ψ(Z_m).
Pieces Y_{m,k} := K_m ∩ {ū_m = g_{m,k}} ∩ ψ⁻¹(M) are Borel with compact closure in V, map into M, and f∘ψ = g_{m,k} on them.
(M ∩ ψ(V)) ∖ ⋃ψ(Y_{m,k}) ⊆ ⋃_m ψ(Z_m) is H^N-null.

subproblems.title: Approximate tangent planes of M along one bi-Lipschitz C¹ chart, off a Borel null set (Simon Ch. 3, Remark 1.5(2), proof of 1.6 '⇒')
subproblems.statement: Let P, N ∈ ℕ and let M ⊆ ℝ^P be Borel with H^N(M ∩ K) < ∞ for every compact K ⊆ ℝ^P (H^N = μHE[N]). Let g : ℝ^N → ℝ^P be C¹, c ∈ ℝ^N, r ∈ ℝ and m > 0 with m|a − b| ≤ |g(a) − g(b)| for all a, b ∈ ball(c, r), and suppose S := g(ball(c, r)) is Borel with H^N(S) < ∞. Then there is a Borel set E ⊆ ℝ^P with H^N(E) = 0 such that for every y ∈ ball(c, r) with g(y) ∈ M and g(y) ∉ E, M has approximate tangent space Dg(y)(ℝ^N) = range(fderiv ℝ g y) at g(y) (SimonGMT HasApproximateTangentSpaceAt N M (g y) (LinearMap.range (fderiv ℝ g y)), Simon Ch. 3, 1.4).
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (P N : ℕ) (M : Set (Euclid P)) (g : Euclid N → Euclid P) (c : Euclid N) (r m : ℝ), MeasurableSet M → (∀ K : Set (Euclid P), IsCompact K → μHE[N] (M ∩ K) ≠ ∞) → ContDiff ℝ 1 g → 0 < m → (∀ a ∈ ball c r, ∀ b ∈ ball c r, m * ‖a - b‖ ≤ ‖g a - g b‖) → MeasurableSet (g '' ball c r) → μHE[N] (g '' ball c r) ≠ ∞ → ∃ E : Set (Euclid P), MeasurableSet E ∧ μHE[N] E = 0 ∧ ∀ y ∈ ball c r, g y ∈ M → g y ∉ E → HasApproximateTangentSpaceAt N M (g y) (LinearMap.range (fderiv ℝ g y : Euclid N →ₗ[ℝ] Euclid P))
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source. Step 8 of the supplied proof of chart_pieces, for a single chart. That is Simon Ch. 3, Remark 1.5(2) and the proof of Theorem 1.6 '⇒' (chapter-03.txt lines 86–90 and 113–146): T_xM = T_xN_j for Hⁿ-a.e. x ∈ M_j. Siblings used:
- c1_piece_tangent (codim1_rdo_c1_piece_approxTangent): the tangent plane of the C¹ disk S. It replaces the closed-ball sibling c1_tangent, because here the chart is an open ball with a lower Lipschitz bound.
- tangent_transfer (doraggt_ae_approxTangent_transfer): the locality TL in its symmetric two-set form, with W = ℝ^P.
Applying TL directly to S and M removes the auxiliary Borel set D_b of the supplied step 8.

1. (Local finiteness.) For every compact K ⊆ ℝ^P, H^N(S ∩ K) ≤ H^N(S) < ∞, and H^N(M ∩ K) < ∞ by hypothesis.

2. (Transfer.) Apply tangent_transfer with W := ℝ^P (open), A := S and B := M. Both are Borel, and step 1 gives the two finiteness hypotheses (for compact K ⊆ W). Conclusion: for H^N-a.e. x ∈ ℝ^P, if x ∈ W, x ∈ S and x ∈ M, then for every linear subspace Q, S has approximate tangent space Q at x iff M does.

3. (Exceptional set.) Let E₀ be the set of x ∈ ℝ^P at which the implication of step 2 fails.
- By the definition of 'almost everywhere', H^N(E₀) = 0 (Mathlib ae_iff).
- Choose a Borel set E ⊇ E₀ with H^N(E) = 0 (Mathlib exists_measurable_superset_of_null).

4. (Conclusion.) Let y ∈ ball(c, r) with g(y) ∈ M and g(y) ∉ E, and put x := g(y).
- Since E₀ ⊆ E, x ∉ E₀, so the implication of step 2 holds at x.
- x ∈ W = ℝ^P; x ∈ S because y ∈ ball(c, r); and x ∈ M. Hence, for every Q, S has approximate tangent space Q at x iff M does.
- By c1_piece_tangent, S has approximate tangent space range(Dg(y)) at g(y). Its hypotheses hold: g is C¹, m > 0, the lower bound holds on ball(c, r), and y ∈ ball(c, r).
Taking Q := range(Dg(y)), M has approximate tangent space range(Dg(y)) = Dg(y)(ℝ^N) at g(y). ∎
proof_key_steps: S = g(ball(c,r)) and M are Borel and locally H^N-finite.
tangent_transfer with W = ℝ^P: for H^N-a.e. x ∈ S ∩ M, S and M have the same approximate tangent spaces at x.
Enlarge the exceptional set to a Borel H^N-null set E.
For y ∈ ball(c,r) with g(y) ∈ M ∖ E, c1_piece_tangent gives T_{g(y)}S = Dg(y)(ℝ^N), which transfers to M.

subproblems.title: Disjointification of countably many injectively parametrised Borel pieces (Simon Ch. 3, Remark 1.3)
subproblems.statement: Let P, N ∈ ℕ. For j ∈ ℕ let ψ_j : ℝ^N → ℝ^P be continuous and Y_j ⊆ ℝ^N Borel with ψ_j injective on Y_j. Then there are Borel sets Y'_j ⊆ Y_j (j ∈ ℕ) such that the images ψ_j(Y'_j) are pairwise disjoint and ⋃_j ψ_j(Y'_j) = ⋃_j ψ_j(Y_j).
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (P N : ℕ) (ψ : ℕ → Euclid N → Euclid P) (Y : ℕ → Set (Euclid N)), (∀ j, Continuous (ψ j)) → (∀ j, MeasurableSet (Y j)) → (∀ j, InjOn (ψ j) (Y j)) → ∃ Y' : ℕ → Set (Euclid N), (∀ j, MeasurableSet (Y' j) ∧ Y' j ⊆ Y j) ∧ Pairwise (fun i j => Disjoint (ψ i '' Y' i) (ψ j '' Y' j)) ∧ ⋃ j, ψ j '' Y' j = ⋃ j, ψ j '' Y j
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source. Step 7 of the supplied proof of chart_pieces. That is Simon Ch. 3, Remark 1.3 (chapter-03.txt lines 68–73): 'just define the M_j inductively by M_0 = M ∩ N_0 and M_j = M ∩ N_j ∖ ⋃_{i<j} M_i … the sets M_j so constructed are all Hⁿ-measurable if M is'. The construction is applied to the image sets and then pulled back to the parameter sets.

1. (Borel images.) A_j := ψ_j(Y_j) is Borel. ℝ^N is Polish, Y_j is Borel, and ψ_j is continuous and injective on Y_j, so the Lusin–Souslin theorem applies (Mathlib MeasurableSet.image_of_continuousOn_injOn).

2. (First-hit sets.) D_j := A_j ∖ ⋃_{i<j} A_i is Borel: a Borel set minus a finite union of Borel sets.

3. (Parameter pieces.) Y'_j := Y_j ∩ ψ_j⁻¹(D_j) ⊆ Y_j. It is Borel, because ψ_j is continuous, hence Borel measurable.

4. (Images.) For any map ψ and sets S, T, ψ(S ∩ ψ⁻¹(T)) = ψ(S) ∩ T. Hence ψ_j(Y'_j) = A_j ∩ D_j = D_j, since D_j ⊆ A_j.

5. (Disjointness.) Let i ≠ j, say i < j. Every x ∈ D_j satisfies x ∉ A_i, while D_i ⊆ A_i; so D_i ∩ D_j = ∅. The case i > j is symmetric. By step 4, ψ_i(Y'_i) and ψ_j(Y'_j) are disjoint.

6. (Same union.)
- ⋃_j D_j ⊆ ⋃_j A_j, since D_j ⊆ A_j.
- Conversely, let x ∈ ⋃_j A_j and let j be the least index with x ∈ A_j. Then x ∉ A_i for all i < j, so x ∈ D_j.
Hence, by step 4, ⋃_j ψ_j(Y'_j) = ⋃_j D_j = ⋃_j A_j = ⋃_j ψ_j(Y_j). ∎
proof_key_steps: A_j = ψ_j(Y_j) is Borel by Lusin–Souslin (continuous and injective on a Borel subset of a Polish space).
D_j := A_j ∖ ⋃_{i<j} A_i are Borel, pairwise disjoint, with the same union as the A_j (least index).
Y'_j := Y_j ∩ ψ_j⁻¹(D_j) is Borel and ψ_j(Y'_j) = D_j.
